strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: online monitoring of equilibrium behavior in multi-agent systems with anytime-valid inference
Theoretically rigorous framework with formal guarantees for error control (FWER in Theorem 2.6, FDR in Theorem 2.8) and detection time bounds (Theorems 2.7, 3.4)
Elegant application of e-value methodology to construct martingale-based tests that enable continuous monitoring without fixed sample sizes
Generalizes beyond Nash equilibrium to correlated and coarse equilibria, and extends from normal-form to stochastic games
Provides concrete algorithmic implementations (Algorithms 1-2) with explicit threshold-setting procedures and careful parameter analysis
weaknesses: Critical assumption of counterfactual payoff access (requires observing u_i(a'_i, a_{-i}) for all alternative actions) is unrealistic and severely limits practical applicability—acknowledged only in Remark 2.10 despite being fundamental
Requires knowing the equilibrium π a priori, and testing requires knowing candidate alternative policies π^(1) in advance, limiting applicability to detecting unforeseen deviations

Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing e-value frameworks (Ramdas et al. 2023, Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2023) to equilibrium monitoring; the conceptual advance over prior equilibrium testing work (Babichenko et al. 2017) is incremental
Theorem 2.6 family-wise error rate bound involves Σ_i |A_i|, creating exponential blow-up with game size and action space—undermines scalability for practical applications
Experiments limited to toy games (2×2, 5×4, 10×10 Predator-Prey) with perfect observations and simple alternative strategies; no evaluation on realistic game sizes or under noisy/partial observations

Proposition 2.4 creates circularity: log-optimal betting fraction λ* = η depends on unknown slack parameter η; practical procedure for setting this remains unclear despite being critical for detection time
Theorem 3.4 requires unrealistic assumptions: process started in stationarity, support conditions requiring detailed knowledge of alternative strategy π^(1)
Dense mathematical exposition obscures key insights and intuition for why e-values solve this problem; presentation of connection between Sections 2 and 3 is abrupt
No comparison to baseline methods (standard hypothesis testing, simpler online detection approaches) or evaluation of robustness to model misspecification
Minimal practical guidance: parameter selection (λ, η, σ) relies on unknown quantities; limited discussion of when practitioners should adopt this over alternatives

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework: Solid application of martingale theory and e-values to develop anytime-valid statistical tests for equilibrium monitoring without fixed sample sizes
Asymptotically optimal detection: Framework achieves O(1/ε²) detection time scaling, matching information-theoretic lower bounds
Comprehensive scope: Covers repeated normal-form games, stochastic games, FWER and FDR control with unified principles
Novel problem formulation: Well-motivated application of sequential testing to detect strategic deviations in multi-agent systems
Detailed theoretical exposition: Complete proofs and extensive appendices enhance reproducibility and enable verification of claims
weaknesses: Critical unrealistic assumption: Requires observing counterfactual payoffs u_i(a_i', a_{-i}) for all deviations, not just realized payoffs. This is infeasible in most real systems (e.g., trading), severely limiting practical applicability

Limited experimental validation: Only toy problems tested (2×2 game, Grid Soccer, Predator-Prey); no real-world applications, no comparisons with alternative methods, missing scalability experiments to larger games

Restrictive knowledge requirements: Framework assumes knowledge of equilibrium π (or specific alternatives π^(1)), state distribution known in stochastic games—unrealistic assumptions not adequately addressed

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 2.7 bound depends on unknown mixture ν (non-constructive); Theorem 3.4 constant C_i not practically computable; no guidance on choosing slack parameter η; arbitrary parameter choices (λ=0.05) with minimal sensitivity analysis

Moderate technical novelty: Core techniques (e-values, martingale tests, likelihood ratios) are well-established; main contribution is combining them rather than developing fundamentally new methods; stochastic game extension is natural but incremental

Presentation issues: Dense exposition reduces accessibility; main results relegated to later sections after extensive setup; heavy notation with multiple subscripts makes tracking difficult; Figures 1-2 hard to interpret

Underdeveloped robustness: No analysis of approximate or unknown equilibria; no discussion of model misspecification; mixture-based approach (Section 3.2) introduced ad-hoc without theoretical justification; continuous case requires strong assumptions not well-justified

strengths: Novel application of e-value framework to equilibrium monitoring, first anytime-valid approach to sequential testing in multi-agent games
Sound mathematical framework with rigorous guarantees (FWER and FDR control, tight detection time bounds)
Improved information requirements compared to prior work (Babichenko et al. 2017): does not require knowledge of equilibrium strategy in normal-form setting
Comprehensive treatment including extensions to correlated/coarse-correlated equilibria, stochastic games, and alternative testing frameworks with detailed proofs
Well-designed FDR control via e-BH procedure with proven speedup over FWER (Proposition 2.9, empirically validated with 1.15× in 2×2 game)
Strong experimental validation of theoretical predictions: O(1/ε²) scaling law (Figure 2) and robustness to unknown deviations (Figure 3)
Reproducibility: code made publicly available with detailed experimental documentation
weaknesses: I.i.d. assumption on joint action profiles is highly restrictive, excluding learning dynamics, correlated strategies, and temporal dependencies common in practice
Requires pre-specification of slack parameter η > 0 (minimum detectable deviation) with no principled guidance for practitioners; this is a practical barrier to adoption

Limited experimental scope: only synthetic games (2×2, 20-player Rock-Paper-Scissors, gridworlds); no real-world validation or comparison to alternative methods (change-point detection, classical corrections)
Gap between Sections 2 and 3: different testing frameworks (regret-based vs likelihood-ratio) weaken the 'unified' contribution claim
Support condition requirement (π_i(a|s) > 0 when π^(1)_i(a|s) > 0) in stochastic games is addressed only via ad-hoc smoothing; adds hyperparameter tuning burden
Practical guidance is missing: no principled methods for selecting α, b, η or analyzing computational complexity; detection times in thousands of rounds
Theoretical optimality of λ* = η does not translate to practice (Section H.1.4 shows larger λ can empirically outperform); discrepancy inadequately discussed
Dense presentation with key material relegated to appendices; intuition for why regret-like increments capture equilibrium violations could be clearer

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with valid anytime-validity guarantees via martingale theory and e-values
Unified treatment of multiple equilibrium concepts (Nash, correlated, coarse correlated) within a single framework
Well-executed extension to stochastic games with state-dependent dynamics via likelihood ratios
FDR control via e-BH procedures (Algorithm 2, Theorem 2.8) provides principled power improvements with rigorous control
Comprehensive theoretical analysis including detection time bounds and comparison to fixed-sample asymptotic rates
Thorough documentation with detailed proofs, alternative frameworks, and extensive experimental details in appendices
weaknesses: Requires unrealistic counterfactual payoff information u_i(a'_i, a_{-i}) in normal-form setting and known policy π in stochastic games; practitioners rarely have access to these
Critical contradiction: paper motivates detecting behavioral drift from learning dynamics, yet assumes i.i.d. action profiles that rule out any learning or adaptation
Slack parameter η selection lacks principled guidance; detection time diverges as η→0 but practitioners don't know appropriate magnitude a priori
Experimental validation limited to toy problems (2×2 games, small gridworlds); no real multi-agent applications or comparison to alternative detection methods
Gap between theory and practice: while asymptotic guarantees are rigorous, they apply to stylized i.i.d. setting that contradicts practical motivation
Support condition (Theorem 3.4) is very restrictive; solution uses ad-hoc smoothing (β=0.05) with unclear impact on detection properties
Missing practical guidance on parameter selection (mixture distribution ν, smoothing parameters) and interpretation of detected deviations
No discussion of computational complexity or comparison to simpler baselines (CUSUM, simpler sequential tests, running-window approaches)

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: First sequential/anytime-valid framework for detecting deviations from game-theoretic equilibria in real time
Sound theoretical framework: Theorems 2.6-2.8 provide FWER/FDR control with expected detection times matching fixed-sample bounds (Theorem 2.7)
Comprehensive scope: Unifies treatment of Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria; extends to stochastic games with state-dependent dynamics
Practical extensions: FDR control (Theorem 2.8, Proposition 2.9) improves power in large games; mixture martingales (Equation 6) provide robustness to unknown deviation magnitudes
Clear presentation and thorough validation: Well-structured main text with detailed appendices; experiments demonstrate FDR vs FWER tradeoff, O(1/ε²) scaling law, and scalability to 20-player games
Elegant theoretical insights: Proposition 2.4 shows optimal betting fraction λ* equals slack parameter η; mixture approach automatically balances sensitivity across deviation magnitudes
weaknesses: Strong information requirements: Normal-form framework requires observable counterfactual payoffs u_i(a'_i, a_{-i}) for all deviations (hard to satisfy in practice without environment model); stochastic framework requires knowledge of target policy π. Practical guidance on which framework to use given available information is lacking

Slack parameter η requires a priori specification with no principled guidance for practitioners: Smaller η requires more rounds; mixture approach helps but doesn't fully resolve the issue. What should practitioners choose in practice?

Gap between theory and practice: Theory assumes exact payoff observations (real systems have noise), strictly stationary i.i.d. play (learning agents exhibit autocorrelation), and observable counterfactuals (requires environmental model). Robustness to assumption violations is not analyzed

Limited experimental baselines: No comparison with Babichenko et al. (2017) or simpler heuristic methods; experiments use synthetic games/gridworlds rather than learned equilibria from actual multi-agent learning systems; practitioners lack clear guidance on when to use this method vs. alternatives

Stochastic games extension feels somewhat disconnected: Pivots from equilibrium testing to compliance testing against specified policy π^(1); Remark 3.5 addresses unknown deviations via mixture but adds complexity. Assumptions of ergodicity and stationary start are restrictive

Practical implementation guidance: How to select λ in practice? How to verify stationarity/i.i.d. assumptions? What is computational complexity? Data-splitting approach (H.2) is somewhat ad-hoc regarding choice of T₀ and K
